title: Sequoia's Former Boss on Reading People: What Happens Before 14 Sets the Core
dek: Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you absorb unconsciously from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.
why: Not an investing lesson but a retrospective on origins, reading people, and writing. The back half — structural shifts in venture and the great man view of history — is the most valuable; the family history up front is more personal.
who: People who evaluate founders, early-stage investors, and angels: those who want to know which of 40 years of people-picking experience still holds and which has expired.
skip: The current-events and antisemitism discussion starting at 11 minutes is more personal opinion and can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: The grandfather who waited for the situation to pass vanished
points.body: Moritz's two grandfathers were two reactions to the same catastrophe. His maternal grandfather was a lower-court judge in Bavaria, had fought at Verdun in World War I, believed in the durability of the state, and had a pension he was unwilling to give up, so he kept delaying his departure and was ultimately sent east with his wife and disappeared from history. The other grandfather was nearly blind, supported the family alone by trading cattle, had no pension to wait for, and left with his wife 72 hours before the war broke out — three days later and they too would have died. Moritz says the lesson he draws is not a moral judgment but that you must always have a bolt hole to hide in, and never too many passports.

points.h: His most effective question makes people cry on the spot
points.body: When he interviews people he always asks one fixed question: looking back, if there were one thing, one action you could have done differently, what would it be. He remembers a person interviewing at Sequoia bursting into tears when asked this — the man was the son of Latino immigrants, had stolen candy from a corner grocery with friends at around age 12, the shopkeeper told his father, and his father dragged him back to the store by the ear and made him apologize and empty his pockets. Years later, asked this question, the first thing he thought of was still the shame he had brought on his family. Moritz says many people conducting interviews are not really listening to the answer.

points.h: He sorted everyone he knew into categories on Zoom
points.body: Inspired by a series about a French village in World War II, he divides people into three categories: resisters, the silent, and collaborators. During the pandemic, in those Zoom meetings with a dozen little windows, he would stare at each person he knew and think: if these people had lived in a French village in the 1940s, who would stay silent, who would resist, who would collaborate. He says resisters are always a tiny minority, because bad things happen in a country precisely because most people stay silent. Asked how many of the people he has invested in would be resisters, he says he would like to think so, but he is not sure.

points.h: The painter gave himself one day off a year
points.body: Frank Auerbach was a refugee from Nazi Germany, and Moritz calls him a total monomaniac: apart from one day off each Christmas at Brighton Pier, he painted every single day. His models were a small fixed group of people, the same few faces painted for decades; one model who lived in Venice flew to London once a week to sit for him. His wife's house was right on the English coast, and Moritz asked whether he went there; he answered: I have never been to that house. From this Moritz discusses the cost of monomania — the cost to relationships is almost inevitable, but sometimes great things come out of exactly there.

points.h: He bet on something beyond the résumé
points.body: Around 1985, Moritz was still a journalist and wrote to five small funds looking for a job. Everyone except Don Valentine told him he had no technical background, no engineering degree, no experience at a tech company, and suggested he go into PR or marketing. Don was willing to take the risk, for a direct reason: he had seen several people with operating backgrounds at large tech companies move into investing and fail, and he had also seen several who succeeded — an actuary, and the one he cited most, Arthur Rock: an investment banker by background, with nothing in his résumé that foreshadowed success. Don did not believe in teaching people; he believed in throwing them into the deep end and seeing whether they drown.

points.h: Venture's old advantage was imperfect information
points.body: Moritz says doing venture in the 1980s and 90s had several advantages that have now disappeared, the first being imperfect information: before the internet, unless you were close to something you did not know what was happening, whereas now the whole world basically gets the same information. The second is that the early market has far too many participants — individuals, two- or three-person funds, giant mutual funds — too many intermediaries, and it is no longer possible for investors to build the kind of real, close relationship with founders they once had. He therefore says a moderately intelligent, quick-minded 14- to 16-year-old could have done venture in the mid-80s; he is not sure he could still do it well today.

points.h: He believes in the great man view of history without apology
points.body: Asked whether it is great individuals or enduring institutions that shape the course of history, Moritz's answer is blunt: he is a firm believer in the great man theory. From Lee Iacocca to Steve Jobs, from politics to the battlefield, what matters is great leaders; and of course also tyrants who cast a shadow over tens of millions of people for decades. In his work at Sequoia and in writing Ferguson, he cares about the same thing — how an organization stays alive across decades. And on Elon, he says he is completely stunned by the scale of his achievements across so many different industries, and thinks he may be the greatest industrialist in American history.

points.h: The more AI writes, the more a human voice is worth
points.body: Moritz says that because AI can easily produce vast amounts of text, excellent writing that cuts through the junk is actually appreciating in value; his definition of excellent writing is ‘a voice you can hear that cannot be mistaken for anyone else's’. The hardest thing for a writer is to get close enough to your own inner feeling and voice that it outweighs the weight of others' expectations — he quotes Joseph Campbell: the privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are, and that is also the hardest thing. He does not consider himself a technologist, and says AI is rarely discussed at home; on employment he is optimistic: people predicted doomsday when the atomic bomb went off, and predicted a genetic revolution creating humans in the 1970s, and neither happened, and this time he thinks more jobs will be created than destroyed.

The inner being doesn't change. The outward intensity changes.
